All seven are optional.

| Claim | Meaning (one line) |
|---|---|
| `iss` | Identifies the principal that issued the JWT. |
| `sub` | Identifies the principal that is the subject of the JWT. |
| `aud` | Identifies the recipients the JWT is intended for. |
| `exp` | Identifies the expiration time on or after which the JWT must not be accepted. |
| `nbf` | Identifies the time before which the JWT must not be accepted. |
| `iat` | Identifies the time at which the JWT was issued. |
| `jti` | Provides a unique identifier for the JWT. |

**Is any of them mandatory?** No. Section 4.1 states:

> "None of the claims defined below are intended to be mandatory to use or implement in all cases, but rather they provide a starting point for a set of useful, interoperable claims."

Each subsection closes with the same line, "Use of this claim is OPTIONAL," and Section 4 adds that "The set of claims that a JWT must contain to be considered valid is context dependent and is outside the scope of this specification." So an application can require specific claims for itself, but the RFC requires none.

Two things that are not claims and so are not in the list above: `typ` and `cty` are JOSE Header parameters (Sections 5.1 and 5.2), not registered claim names. `cty` is the one place the document makes something mandatory — it "MUST be present" with value "JWT" when nested signing or encryption is used.
